name: The Rybczynski Theorem
statement: At constant goods prices, an increase in one factor's endowment expands the output of the sector using it intensively and absolutely shrinks the other sector's output.
statementAccent: an increase in one factor's endowment expands the output of the sector using it intensively
meaning: The theorem describes how, holding relative goods prices fixed, growth in the supply of one production factor causes a more-than-proportional expansion of the industry that uses that factor intensively, while the other industry’s output falls in absolute terms. It is one of the four core theorems within the Heckscher–Ohlin model.
mechanism: With two goods, two factors, and fixed relative prices, factor prices must stay fixed to preserve zero profits, which pins down each industry’s factor intensities. The extra unit of the abundant factor must be absorbed by the sector using it intensively, which draws the other, unchanged factor away from the other sector, forcing that sector’s output to contract.

examples.text: Polish-born British economist Tadeusz Rybczynski formulated the theorem in 1955, showing a rise in one factor’s endowment raises the output of the good using it intensively and lowers the other good’s output in absolute terms.

If a country’s labour supply grows while capital is unchanged, labour-intensive industries such as clothing expand more than proportionally, while capital-intensive industries such as automobiles contract in absolute output.
The theorem is linked to "Dutch disease," where a resource discovery — a factor-endowment increase — expands the resource sector while other tradable sectors such as manufacturing contract.

whyItMatters: It explains how changes in a country’s factor supplies — capital inflows, immigration, resource discoveries — reshape the composition of domestic output even without any change in world prices, underpinning analyses of immigration’s sectoral effects and resource-driven deindustrialisation.
limits: The theorem depends on the same restrictive two-good, two-factor, fixed-price assumptions as the rest of the Heckscher–Ohlin model, and strictly requires relative goods prices to remain constant — a condition often violated when factor-endowment shocks are large enough to move world prices.
misreadings: It is sometimes confused with simply predicting that all sectors grow when a factor grows; instead it uniquely predicts an absolute decline in the other sector’s output.
origin: Formulated by Polish-born British economist Tadeusz Rybczynski (1923–1998) in a 1955 article, within the Heckscher–Ohlin framework.

sources.text: Rybczynski theorem, Wikipedia. — the statement, its 1955 origin, and the Dutch-disease connection.
Tadeusz Rybczynski, Wikipedia. — his identity and dates as the theorem’s namesake.
